lesson.menu_title: The Final Calibration — Sounding Like Yourself
lesson.menu_desc: Short answers, one fact and a hand back, so the second interview sounds like a conversation -- 33 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 20 -- The Final Calibration
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Fernando Meneghelli Bottura | Lesson 20 -- The Final Calibration

listenings.text: When I give feedback to a candidate after a first round, the most common note is the same: your answers were right, but they were long. Senior people over-explain because they have prepared so much, and they want to use all of it. So when the panel asks a yes or no question, they repeat the whole question back, add the context, and then the answer arrives at the end. In the second round, I tell them to try something simple. If the question is have you done this, start with I have, or I haven't. Then give one fact, and stop. It feels too short to them. To the panel, it sounds like somebody who is sure of the answer.

I have interviewed a lot of finance directors whose English was better than mine, and some of them still sounded stilted. They spoke in complete paragraphs. If I asked whether they would relocate, I got a speech about family and career. The candidate I hired last year did something different. I asked if he expected the market to recover, and he said, I think so, but not before the autumn. I asked if he had ever lost a client, and he said, I have, and I would rather tell you how we won the next one. It was a real back-and-forth. I stopped interviewing him and started talking to him, and that is usually the moment I decide.

extra_audio.text: Joanna asks if he found the office all right, and he says he did. She asks if he has ever run finance for a business that was being sold, and he says he has, once. He says he would do it again, if the board was clear about the timetable. She asks if the team is strong enough, and he says he thinks so. Finally, he mentions one small concern: the reporting line.

paras: Interviewers who hire senior finance people say the same thing about a certain kind of candidate: everything was correct, and nothing was natural. The numbers were right, the stories were well built, and yet the conversation never started. The candidate answered questions; he did not talk to anybody.

The cause is usually preparation, not the lack of it. A candidate who has rehearsed every answer wants to use all of it. Asked a yes or no question, he repeats the question, gives the context, and arrives at the answer a minute later. To the panel this comes across as long-winded, and sometimes as defensive, even when the content is excellent.

The candidates who build rapport do something smaller. They answer the question first, often in two or three words: I have. I think so. I hope not. They add one fact, and then they stop and let the interviewer decide whether she wants more. Several interviewers described this as the moment an interview becomes a back-and-forth, and one chief executive said it is usually the moment she decides.
None of this means preparing less. The best candidates prepare the content in detail and then strike a balance in the room: the facts are rehearsed, the sentences are not.
reading.source: Adapted from interviewer notes on senior finance appointments

choices: Candidates should prepare much less, so that every answer in the interview sounds spontaneous and off the cuff.
Well-prepared candidates often sound rehearsed; short answers with one fact turn the interview into a conversation.
Interviewers only care about the numbers.
